extracted.intended_audience: students and teachers of poetry, literary critics, and readers learning close reading
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating poems by close reading: identifying the poet's intended effects, testing sincerity, assessing imagery, form, diction, rhythm, and avoiding personal/stock responses. Shows how readers' reactions map to critical standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discover the poet's intended effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Attempt to discover what effects the poet was trying to get.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism should try to identify the poet's aims and the emotional, imagistic, or intellectual effects intended rather than imposing unrelated interpretations. (Referenced in 8.45 and elsewhere as a primary critical task.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Closeness of reading / avoid projecting oneself
rubrics_metrics.description: How near the reader comes to the actual poem rather than imputing their own personality or imagining unrelated scenes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers who imagine scenarios not supported by the text (e.g. thinking a woman is singing onstage) have not 'approached closely' to the poem; such projection lessens the force of their strictures (see 8.45, 8.72).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity versus cheap sentimentality
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether expressed feeling is genuinely sincere or merely cheap/sloshy sentiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The writer introducing familiar sentimental images (old Sunday evenings, hymns, dusk, little child) must be very sure of sincerity and expressive capability to avoid cheap sentimentality; the same imagery can be successful if handled with truthfulness (8.52, 8.6, 8.7).

rubrics_metrics.name: Expression as evidence of sincerity
rubrics_metrics.description: Insincere emotion betrays itself by slovenly or careless expression; precise craft can evidence sincerity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An insincere emotion shows through shoddy phrasing; conversely deft craftsmanship can sometimes conceal insincerity (8.51). This is a test but not infallible (craft can elude the test).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition and dispelling of sentimental danger
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the poet recognise the danger of sentimentality and deliberately avoid exploiting it?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poets who are self-aware about sentimentality and 'recognise and dispel that danger' (8.51) are favourably judged; self-conscious restraint or justness of expression can convert potential sentiment into value (8.7).

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy and simplicity of expression
rubrics_metrics.description: Simplicity and accuracy in recording feelings and justness of expression (not over-pitching) are positive qualities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not 'pitching the thing up' and using just, accurate wording helps the poem succeed in doing what it sets out to do (8.7, 8.71).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of reading other poems / irrelevance
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics should not mistake associations or private reminiscences for features of the poem under consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some readers describe other poems 'floating in private limbo' instead of discovering what the poet is doing; such mnemonic/irrelevant associations undermine critical closeness (8.72, introduction to later sets).

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability/aptness of similes and metaphors
rubrics_metrics.description: Similes and imagery must be suitable, not awkward or meaningless for the context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers complained when similes seemed unsuitable (e.g., Alpine peaks when drinking in a crowd), far-fetched metaphors, or images that do not cohere with the situation (9.12, 9.71–9.77).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of diction to subject
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether high-flown or particular word-choices are justified by the poem's subject and aim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Questions arise like 'Does the subject justify the rather high-flown language?' or whether words are used merely to fill a rhyme (examples: 'guide' as rhyme choice) (9.17, 8.61).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fit of subject to formal type (form appropriateness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the chosen subject is appropriate to the poem's formal type (e.g., sonnet, dramatic piece, toast).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some readers feel a 'health unto the king' is outside their notion of sonnet content or that certain subjects demand different rhythms; others argue subject and sonnet are both dignified and fit (9.82–9.83).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evocation of mood and emotional contagion
rubrics_metrics.description: The poem's ability to communicate its mood so that the reader shares the poet's feeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Praises focus on contagious exhilaration or warmth; if the poet's mood is infectious and moves the reader, the poem fulfills a key demand of poetry (9.5, 9.31, 9.9).

rubrics_metrics.name: Power and vividness of visual imagery and colour
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of colour and vivid images that produce strong mental pictures is a major source of attraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lines evoking colour (e.g., 'crimson wine', 'colours of the sea-shell') appeal to readers' sense of colour and the mind's eye; some regard such pictorial strength as a principal merit (9.4, 9.41–9.44).

rubrics_metrics.name: Musical qualities: metre, rhythm, and phrasing
rubrics_metrics.description: Meter, rhythm, rhyme, alliteration and musical phrasing should suit the poem's mood and movement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers note when metre doesn't scan, when rhythm emphasises reflection, or when phrasing has swing; musical appropriateness can both support or undermine the poem's effect (8.61, 9.31, 9.71, Poem 10 notes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality vs exploitation of conventional / stock responses
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the poem exploits conventional associations or evokes fresh, original response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics accuse some poems of using 'customary apparatus of poetical hackwork' or conventional similes; the central question is if the poem earns the right to exploit those associations (9.92–9.93).

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical accuracy and internal scansion
rubrics_metrics.description: Technical correctness: scansion, word fit for metre/rhyme, and factual/technical detail where relevant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers point out metrical faults (line 3 stanza i not scanning), poor rhyme-driven diction (e.g., 'guide'), or technical inaccuracies (9.21 1 about how to drink wine); such matters can weaken judgement but are sometimes secondary to effect (8.61, 9.211).

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity vs artifice (craft without substance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish genuine expressive power from clever versification that masks lack of substance ('a clever fake').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A poem may show high technical skill—completeness of pattern, alliteration—but still be judged empty or 'verbal flatulence' if it lacks real content (9.3).

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal coherence of imagery and facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Imagery must be coherent within its internal facts (e.g., temporal or sensory contradictions should be noticed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics point out impossibilities like Dawn listening to lightning of spring nights or simultaneous images that can't co-exist (9.76–9.77). Such incoherence may make imagery seem far-fetched.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form recognition and performance considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognise if poem is essentially dramatic or intended for performance; some pieces are best judged when heard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some readers see dramatic pieces that require declamation or performance to be fully appreciated (9.8–9.81). Failure to recognise form can lead to inappropriate expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Awareness of personal prejudice and associations
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers' private associations, political sympathies, or personal habits can colour judgement and should be accounted for.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: royalist or republican sympathies changing reception of 'King' (9.14–9.15); a teetotaller reacting to wine imagery (9.22). Critics should note such biases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptability of hyperbole and emotive, non-illustrative similes
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether hyperbole or emotive similes are justified by the poem's sincerity and nobility of sentiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hyperbole may sound hollow but can be justified when it expresses an inexpressible emotion sincerely (9.91). The critic must judge whether the emotional weight earns the hyperbole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reader's mnemonic pull and personal memory (as suspect evidence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Be cautious treating mnemonic or nostalgic responses as objective evidence of a poem's quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers' proud recollections or mnemonic pleasure (e.g., wanting to sing aloud) may explain liking but are not definitive critical proof; mnemonic appeal can mislead (Poem 10 notes, 10.2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of matter, mood, and movement (means to ends)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether matter, mood, and structural movement correspond and whether means are well-suited to the poet's aim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Praise and dispraise often align along whether the poet suited his means to his end; those who object to the aim quarrel with the means (9.31 discussion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge imagery not only for lucidity but for emotive function
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognise that some similes are emotive (evoking feeling) rather than explanatory, and judge them on that basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some figurative language aims to produce emotion rather than clarify; critics must distinguish emotive similes from attempts at elucidation and judge accordingly (final paragraph on hyperbole and emotive similes).
